q: According to the chapter, the last two years of British rule witnessed two basic strands of national upsurge. Which of the following correctly describes them?
o: Purely peaceful negotiations with no mass action whatsoever
Complete absence of any negotiations, with only violent mass uprisings
Tortuous negotiations among government, Congress and League culminating in freedom and partition; and sporadic, militant mass action by workers, peasants and states' peoples
A single unified armed rebellion led jointly by the Congress and the League

q: What was the most significant feature of the Congress's 1945-46 election campaign strategy?
o: It was conducted entirely in cooperation with the Muslim League
It sought to mobilise Indians against the British rather than merely appealing for votes, glorifying Quit India martyrs and condemning repressive officials
It avoided any mention of the 1942 movement to prevent provoking the government
It focused exclusively on economic promises to voters with no reference to nationalism

q: Regarding the INA trials, which of the following is correct?
o: The trials were held in strict secrecy with no public knowledge of the accused
Only Muslim INA officers were put on trial by the British
The first trial, held at the Red Fort in Delhi in November 1945, controversially placed a Hindu (Sehgal), a Muslim (Shah Nawaz Khan) and a Sikh (Dhillon) together in the dock
The trials were held in Singapore rather than in India

q: Which of the following prominent lawyers organised the legal defence of INA prisoners in court?
o: M.A. Jinnah and Liaqat Ali Khan exclusively
Only Jawaharlal Nehru, acting alone as defence counsel
C. Rajagopalachari and Vallabhbhai Patel exclusively
Bhulabhai Desai, Tej Bahadur Sapru, Kailash Nath Katju, Jawaharlal Nehru and Asaf Ali

q: Which of the following groups extended support to the INA cause, apart from the Congress?
o: Only the Congress supported the INA cause; all other parties opposed it
Solely the Communist Party, with all other groups remaining neutral
The Muslim League, Communist Party, Unionists, Akalis, Justice Party, RSS, Hindu Mahasabha and the Sikh League
The British government itself formally endorsed the INA cause

q: Which of the following correctly lists the three major upsurges of the winter of 1945-46?
o: The Tebhaga movement, the Telangana revolt, and the Worli revolt
The Quit India Movement, the Individual Satyagraha, and the Civil Disobedience Movement
Calcutta (Nov 21, 1945) over INA trials; Calcutta (Feb 11, 1946) over Rashid Ali's sentence; Bombay RIN ratings' strike (Feb 18, 1946)
Bombay riots (1946), Noakhali riots (1946), and Bihar riots (1946)

q: According to the chapter's evaluation, what was a key limitation of the three 1945-46 upsurges despite their significance?
o: They were short-lived, confined to a few urban centres, and the communal unity displayed was more organisational (Muslims consulting the League, others the Congress) than a genuine unity among the people
They were entirely orchestrated and directed by the Congress leadership from the start
They had no impact whatsoever on British policy or concessions
They failed to attract any participation from the armed forces at all

q: What was Gandhi's opinion on the RIN mutiny of February 1946?
o: He called for the ratings to be given full political power immediately
He fully endorsed and praised the mutiny as the ideal method of struggle
He was indifferent and made no comment on the mutiny
He felt the mutiny was badly advised — wrong if aimed at fighting for freedom without guidance, and wrong if it was over grievances since the ratings should have waited for leaders' guidance

q: In the 1945-46 elections, which of the following describes the Congress's performance?
o: It won a majority of Muslim votes across all provinces
It captured all 102 seats in the Central Assembly
It lost every provincial election held during this period
It won 91% of non-Muslim votes, captured 57 of 102 Central Assembly seats, and secured majorities in most provinces except Bengal, Sindh and Punjab

q: In the same elections, which of the following describes the Muslim League's performance?
o: It won only a small minority of Muslim votes and failed to establish itself as representative of Muslims
It won a majority in Punjab outright without any coalition
It performed identically to its poor 1937 showing
It won 86.6% of Muslim votes, captured all 30 reserved Central Assembly seats, and won majorities in Bengal and Sindh, firmly establishing itself as the dominant Muslim party unlike in 1937

q: Why did the 1945-46 elections show strong communal voting patterns despite the anti-British unity displayed in the mass upsurges of the same period?
o: Due to separate electorates and a highly limited franchise (under 10% for provinces, under 1% for the Central Assembly)
Because the Congress and League contested on a joint platform
Because voting was entirely voluntary and open to all adults regardless of religion
Because the British banned all communal parties from contesting

q: How many members were envisaged for the Constituent Assembly under the Cabinet Mission Plan, and how were they to be apportioned?
o: 250 members nominated solely by the British government
100 members equally divided between Congress and League
389 members — 292 from provincial assemblies, 4 from chief commissioners' provinces, and 93 from princely states
500 members elected entirely by adult suffrage

q: How did the Congress and the Muslim League differ in their interpretation of the Cabinet Mission's 'grouping' clause?
o: The League saw grouping as optional while the Congress insisted it was compulsory
Both parties agreed grouping was entirely optional from the outset
Both parties agreed grouping was compulsory from the outset
The Congress saw grouping as optional (making Pakistan effectively rejected), while the League insisted it was compulsory, implying Pakistan; the Mission later clarified in the League's favour

q: What was Wavell's 'Breakdown Plan' presented to the Cabinet Mission in May 1946?
o: A plan proposing complete merger of Congress and the Muslim League
A plan to permanently retain British rule over all of India
A plan to hold immediate general elections under adult franchise before any transfer of power
A plan envisaging British withdrawal to Muslim-majority North-West and North-East provinces while handing over the rest of the country to the Congress

q: What triggered the Muslim League's withdrawal of its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission's long-term plan on July 29, 1946?
o: Nehru's July 10, 1946 statement suggesting the Constituent Assembly was sovereign and that grouping might not occur since NWFP and Assam would object to joining sections B and C
The resignation of Lord Wavell as Viceroy
The Congress's rejection of the interim government proposal
A unilateral British decision to cancel the Cabinet Mission Plan entirely

q: Which areas were worst affected by the communal riots that erupted from August 16, 1946?
o: Delhi and Madras exclusively
Only Punjab and NWFP
Calcutta, Bombay, Noakhali, Bihar and Garhmukteshwar (United Provinces)
Only princely states, with British India remaining calm

q: When did the Muslim League join the Interim Government, and under what conditions?
o: December 9, 1946, only after formally renouncing Direct Action
It never joined the Interim Government at all
October 26, 1946, without giving up 'direct action' and despite rejecting the Cabinet Mission's plans and insisting on compulsory grouping
September 2, 1946, alongside the Congress from the very start

q: Why did the Muslim League boycott the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly on December 9, 1946?
o: Because the meeting was postponed indefinitely by the Viceroy

As part of its obstructionist approach after rejecting the Cabinet Mission's plans, seeking to use its foothold in government to continue the fight for Pakistan rather than participate in constitution-making
Because the Assembly denied Muslims any representation whatsoever
Because the Congress refused to allow League members to attend

q: According to the chapter, what was the social/class basis of communalism, as argued from a Left perspective?
o: It was rooted in the rising middle classes propagating imaginary communal interests to further their own economic interests, making it 'a bourgeois question par excellence'
It arose purely and exclusively from religious doctrine with no economic basis
It originated solely among industrial workers competing over factory wages
It was entirely a peasant-driven, grassroots phenomenon with no elite involvement

q: Which of the following is cited as a socio-economic reason for the growth of communalism among Muslims?
o: Muslims controlled the majority of India's industrial capital
Muslims were uniformly wealthier and more educated than Hindus across all regions
There was no economic dimension whatsoever to the rise of communalism
Muslims lagged in modern education, trade and industry, leaving educated Muslims dependent on government jobs, which reactionary landlords and loyalist leaders exploited to build communal influence

q: What was the British policy of 'divide and rule' regarding Muslims after the 1870s?
o: The British consistently repressed Muslims throughout without any change in policy
The British granted Muslims complete political independence from British India
Reversing earlier repression, the government began courting Muslims through concessions and favours (via figures like Syed Ahmed Khan) to counter rising nationalism among the educated middle classes
The British banned all Muslim political organisations after 1870

q: How did communal historiography distort India's historical narrative, according to the chapter?
o: It was developed exclusively by nationalist historians with no colonial influence

It portrayed the ancient period as a purely 'Hindu' golden age and the medieval period (Turkish, Afghan, Mughal rule) as a 'Muslim' phase, exaggerating ruling-class conflicts as Hindu-Muslim conflicts
It correctly emphasised that medieval politics was based on religious rather than economic or political interests
It denied any distinction between ancient and medieval periods of Indian history

q: Which of the following are cited as socio-religious reform movements whose militant overtones contributed to communalism?
o: The Brahmo Samaj and the Aligarh Movement
The Self-Respect Movement and the Justice Party
The Wahabi Movement among Muslims and the Shuddhi movement among Hindus
The Ramakrishna Mission and the Theosophical Society

q: Which of Tilak's initiatives is cited as an example of how militant nationalism inadvertently acquired a Hindu communal tinge?
o: The formation of the Congress Socialist Party
The Home Rule Movement
The launch of the Kesari newspaper
The Ganapati and Shivaji festivals along with anti-cow slaughter campaigns

q: According to the chapter, what unease did the Khilafat agitation (1920-22) create among some Congressmen?
o: It was seen as entirely a secular economic agitation with no religious content
The fight was framed around protecting the Caliph and Islamic holy places rather than the economic and political consequences of imperialism, raising concerns about its purely nationalistic character
It was universally regarded as the most successful and unproblematic Congress-led campaign
It received no Muslim participation at all

q: The All India Muslim League was founded in 1906 by which group of leaders, with the initial aim of preaching loyalty to the British government?
o: Iqbal, Jinnah and the Agha Khan jointly
Syed Ahmed Khan, Badruddin Tyabji and Hamid Ali Khan
The Agha Khan, Nawab Salimullah of Dacca, Nawab Mohsin-ul-Mulk and Nawab Waqar-ul-Mulk
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Liaqat Ali Khan and Rahmat Ali

q: What were Jinnah's 'Fourteen Points' (1929), presented in response to the Nehru Report?
o: A programme for Hindu-Muslim unity based on joint electorates
A demand for complete abolition of communal representation
A set of demands including separate electorates and reservation for Muslims in government service and self-governing bodies
A blueprint for the immediate creation of Pakistan as a separate sovereign state

q: What impossible demand did Jinnah make between 1937 and 1939 that blocked avenues for Congress-League conciliation?
o: That the Congress declare itself a Hindu organisation and recognise the Muslim League as the sole representative of Indian Muslims
That all princely states be immediately merged into British India
That the Congress accept dominion status as a permanent constitutional arrangement
That the British immediately grant full independence with no transitional period

q: During the Second World War negotiations (August Offer, Cripps proposals, Shimla Conference, Cabinet Mission), what advantage did the Muslim League consistently exploit?
o: A virtual veto given to it by the British Indian government on any political settlement
Sole representation of India at Allied war conferences
Direct control over the Indian Army's command structure
Complete financial control over the war effort
